utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Thomas Laugel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic with legal assistant, Liane Aronchick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Susa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Olmsted, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we have on the screen, 65 ter 3120.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, good morning.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to return to the issue of the 9 October 1991 decision by the SBWS Great National Assembly, the place the SBWS TO under the -- or within the armed forces of the SFRY. What we have in front of us, if we could enlarge the original a little bit, is a 10 October 1991 letter from Ilija Koncarevic to the SFRY vice-president, Branko Kostic. And we see that this letter was sent one day after the -- the 9 October decision. Mr. Kostic -- or Mr. Koncarevic notes in the first paragraph that the Great National Assembly adopted a decision declaring the district an autonomous federal unit of the new Yugoslav state union. He then provides the substance of the 9 October decision, again, using the term "armed forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. KONCAREVIC THEN STATES
utterances.text: "The Grand National Assembly deems that these two decisions give full legitimacy to the SBWS to be directly and equally represented in the Presidency of Yugoslavia." Mr. Susa, that was the ultimate purpose of the 9 October decision, wasn't it, to place the TO within the armed forces in order to provide a basis for the SBWS to be given a seat within the SFRY Presidency.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think a much more intensive decision was when we joined the Presidency, and putting it in the framework of the TO in order to achieve, would not have been so good. It would have been a -- an inadequate approach to the problem. But specifically this letter of Mr. Koncarevic is not familiar to me. In my view, this decision to resubordinate TO to the JNA was the key decision of that assembly session. The rest is just political theorizing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I believe you've already testified that it was Mr. Koncarevic who was negotiating this 9 October 1991 decision with the SFRY authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That was within his authority as president of the Grand National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you were also aware that it was one of the goals of the SBWS Grand National Assembly and Mr. Koncarevic to obtain a seat for the SBWS in the SFRY Presidency; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I knew that our ultimate goal was to remain a part of Yugoslavia, but I did not know about this aspiration to get our own MP in the assembly. I didn't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I did not say an MP in the assembly. What I said was a seat within the SFRY Presidency.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand you completely. Our wish was to remain a part of Yugoslavia. Perhaps not as a federal unit. That would have been too ambitious but as a territory with a special status. That, certainly. I did not know that there were any ambitions to have a seat on the Presidency. Maybe that was discussed by an narrow circle of people of which I was not a part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's look at 65 ter 6683. This is tab 171. I'd like to draw your attention to the short article that's right in the middle of this newspaper page. And this is a 16 October 1991 Politika article entitled: "Request of the government of the Serbian District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can enlarge the middle -- the middle -- yes, to the left. The short one that's in the box to the left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I see it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. This article reports that Mr. Hadzic told Tanjug: "The Serbian people in this district who are outside the Republic of Serbia, and now they are in Krajina, which means they are no longer in Croatia, should have their representative at the highest level of the country in which they want to be." And if we can look further down in the article, Mr. Hadzic states: "It was logical for the Serbian District of SBWS to have its representative in the country it recognises, whether with equal or other status." Mr. Susa, that was the position of the SBWS government and Mr. Hadzic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, a more important part of the text is the one you haven't read. I, as a member of the government, bore in mind primarily that paragraph, which says we don't want to be a federal unit but we do want to be independent in any case. All these stories about being represented in the Presidency or any other federal body, such as the assembly, were not very present in my mind. Maybe, as I told you before, this was discussed by some other officials of ours, maybe even Goran Hadzic. I don't know. In any case, to me, it doesn't matter. As far as I'm concerned all our policy boiled down to the formulation I've just read. Let us allow the possibility that some of them even had ambitions of being represented in the federal bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 3120 and 6683.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I object to -- to -- to -- because there is no foundation to -- for tendering these documents, since the witness doesn't know anything about the contents of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the witness may take off his headphones for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your headphones, Mr. Susa, for a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution is not surprised that the witness contradicts the Prosecution's propositions being put to him; he is, after all, a Defence witness. But these documents do contradict what this witness has said about the purpose of the 9 October 1991 decision, placing the SBWS TO within the SFRY armed forces. They're right around the same time period that decision was issued and they provide context to that. Now the witness has testified that Mr. Koncarevic was the one who was behind the 9 October decision, so a letter from Mr. Koncarevic is very relevant to this issue. And this article that is now in front of us the Prosecution will submit is closely related to that letter by Mr. Koncarevic. The witness is not, of course, being helpful on this issue because he is standing by his position to what the 9 October 1991 decision was all about. But the Prosecution position is that this document is -- these two documents are necessary for the Trial Chamber to weigh the evidence of this witness as well as to put that evidence within its proper context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My objection is not on the ground of relevancy but on the ground of lack of nexus between the statement of this witness and tendering of these two documents, and I've said that there is no foundation for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. The documents are admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 6683 will be Exhibit P3309. And 3120 will be Exhibit P3310.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, the SFRY Presidency never gave the SBWS a seat on the Presidency, did it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Nor did the SFRY Presidency adopt the Grand National Assembly's 9 October decision and, as a result, the SBWS TO was never incorporated into the SFRY armed forces; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: De facto, it was definitely incorporated into the SFRY armed forces. That's how it operated on the ground. I don't know, though, whether there was a particular decision of the Presidency governing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in your Dokmanovic testimony, you testified that you believed that this 9 October decision was disseminated to the various TO units in the SBWS through the radio, press and television; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, but that was not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, in fact, it's your evidence that even after this 9 October decision, it took effort on the part of the members of the SBWS government to explain to local TO units why it was necessary to places themselves under the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only a smaller number of individuals who opposed it because they felt they were losing their local authority. However, they opposed it without any effect. In the end, they had to be resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's also the case that the local TO commanders always found ways of retaining their autonomy from the JNA; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't always found -- find ways. They tried, but they rarely succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I suppose I need go to your Dokmanovic testimony then. Which you don't have in front of you but I will read to you.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm referring to your Dokmanovic testimony which you do not have in front of you. This is 1 --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is 1D2319 and I'm interested in page 11 in the e-court. And during your Dokmanovic testimony you were being asked about this 9 October decision, and the Defence counsel asked you: "Does this mean that after the 10th of October, the village watches had nothing to do with you?" And on the next page, page 12, you said: "This need not be true in absolute terms because the village watches always found ways of retaining their autonomy with the local commanders." And you go on to say that this is a problem for the JNA? That was your testimony in Dokmanovic. Do you stand by it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still say that. That did not happen everywhere. It happened in individual cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you name the individual cases?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think they were in any way important. It was probably in areas where those local commanders had a lot of power to decide about movements in their territory. That affected their power also to control economic flows, and they were afraid they would lose that position. Those were various and individual cases that I cannot cite now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: There was also a question whether the JNA would ultimately agree to place these local TO units under its command; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early days, that question existed, but later, it happened. The JNA did place TO units under its command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, if you could turn to paragraph 36 of your 2014 statement. It's correct that you do not know to what extent, if any, the local TO units were placed or resubordinated to the JNA; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were. To what extent, I don't know, and I cannot testify about that. That was not within my remit. Fundamentally, it's true they were resubordinated. If there were any exceptions, I don't know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Indeed, under paragraph 36 of your statement after mentioning that the decision was reported to the radio and television, you state: "I also suppose" -- "I also suppose that later on the ground men from the JNA started slowly disarming and resubordinating to them, the units that had, until then, commanded themselves." So you had no direct information whether TO units were being resubordinated to the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no direct information. Only what I saw in the field and hearsay from other people or perhaps even briefings at government sessions. Personally, I did not deal with this. It was not within my job description.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now in your 1998 statement you describe how in the SBWS everything was regulated by law and sublegal acts which you drafted on behalf of the SBWS government and you also stated that the legislative documents were of high quality, at that time higher even of those of Serbia. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those documents that were drafted in the Ministry of Justice, we tried to draft according to the highest available standards. We were able to change some things in law that were very rigid in Serbia, such as economic sanctions, et cetera, but, in the rest, my -- my ministry did not take any part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The laws and regulations for the SBWS were published in official gazettes that were first published in Beli Manastir and then, once the RSK was formed, in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the Beli Manastir municipality also published its decisions in official gazettes also published in Beli Manastir; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had their own municipal official gazette that had nothing to do with our Official Gazette except that the same print works produced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And those gazettes, the SBWS and Beli Manastir gazettes, were available to the public to the extent that they wanted to review them; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should have been available and only those people were duty-bound to read them who, under the law, had to act in accordance with what was published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Last week you testified that the Beli Manastir Executive Council decisions that you described as discriminatory "should have been repealed or harmonised." In fact, they never were repealed by the SBWS government, were they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government did not have to repeal it. They had an imperative order to do it themselves, and in future, to enforce only the laws of the district. And if they failed to do that, I believe they were in conflict with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You can't state that the Beli Manastir Executive Council ever repealed its decisions that it rendered in 1991. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they made an explicit decree repealing them, I don't know. But for me, it's enough that there is a legal enactment under which all their previous decisions had to be considered as inferior to laws. They had to be considered as bylaws, as, as such, they would not be enforced. They would not be applicable.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What legal provocations are he referring to because we have the Official Gazettes for the SBWS and there's nothing in there, as far as I'm aware, which explicitly repeals Executive Council decisions?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is understood that when a law is passed that applies to the entire territory, and the territory of Baranja was in no way excepted, these laws apply mandatorily to the whole territory and thus to Baranja as well. They had to enforce these laws too and if they failed to do so, of which I had no particular evidence, then they would have been in conflict with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, which laws are you referring to that you were in conflict with the Beli Manastir Executive Council decisions?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question begs a very general answer that is very delicate. All the laws --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Witness, if you could please slow down a bit for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. All these laws - and I confirmed it was a large number of laws - had to be enforced by everybody. I don't know which of these laws they failed to apply. You would have to give me a specific example, and then I would be able to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see that there is no -- in transcript the laws that the witness alleged. He enumerated approximately three or maybe four laws. He was --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you list the laws that you mentioned so that we can look them up ourselves to see if they're inconsistent with the Beli Manastir decisions.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I invoke the decision of the Assembly in Beli Manastir. All the laws that were adopted at that time. I cannot even enumerate them all now. All of them at the time of their passing at the Grand National Assembly were adopted, published and had to be applied. If you want me to enumerate them all I will try, but there are certainly 15 to 20 and I'm sure to miss a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But we're only talking about laws that you claim contradicted the decisions by the Beli Manastir Executive Council. But if you cannot point us to those particular laws, that's fine. But you will agree, Mr. Susa, that the -- those Beli Manastir decisions that you proclaimed as discriminatory were consistent with your 11 February 1992 memorandum to the Mohovo local commune?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the decisions of the Beli Manastir municipal council differ considerably from this decision that I sent to the local commune of Mohovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified last week that the SBWS government proposed to the Grand National Assembly to proclaim a state of emergency but that the assembly never acted on that proposal. Now, the reason the assembly did not act on that proposal was that the reason behind it, to introduce work obligation, could be accomplished without a state of emergency; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly took a position on that point, yes. That could have been done without introducing work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 1065. This is tab 50. And these are minutes of the 4/5 May 1992 RSK Assembly -- or RSK government session in Beli Manastir. And you attended this session, correct, we see your name listed?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2 in both the original and the English. We see that after the security briefing from Milan Martic and a discussion that included Minister Spanovic, Minister Veizovic, you and others, the RSK government decided to send a proposal to the republic president to proclaim a state of emergency in the territory of the RSK. Mr. Susa, a state of emergency existed at least as of May 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that a state of emergency was not introduced. A proposal to introduce a state of emergency and to pass a decision on that, it's not one and the same thing. When you asked me a moment ago, I spoke about the situation. We did not speak about the actual time involved. We talked about the situation in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and then the Grand National Assembly refused to introduce a state of emergency. It was Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic that had launched that initiative. I see that the topic that is discussed here has to do with the Republic of the Serb Krajina. We were no longer in the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. There was a proposal here sent to the president. Now whether the president took that into account, we have to see that on the basis of his decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 1065 will be Exhibit P3311.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Susa, please allow me to skip around a little bit in time, because I have limited time and I want to make sure I cover all the issues. In January 1993, Mr. Hadzic exercised his presidential powers by declaring a state of war in the RSK and at the same time he declared a general mobilisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is evident from the documentation. Yes, I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified last week that no one from the SBWS was involved in writing the RSK constitution that was adopted in Borovo Selo in December of 1991. Now, if we look at your statement from 2014, in paragraph 165, you state that: "The Ministry of Justice and Administration of the SBWS and I, myself, were involved in drafting the 19 December 1991 constitution." You've changed your evidence, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I absolutely stand by what I stated. We took part in drafting the constitution. However, that draft constitution was not discussed by the assembly in Borovo Selo. A completely new term was introduced. This constitution that was adopted in Borovo Selo had its shortcomings. We would have never allowed ourselves to say in the constitution that the Republic of the Serb Krajina would be established only in the territory of the Krajina and further on, of course, I stood by that, that we worked on a concept of the constitution that was not a subject of discussion. Everything that we prepared beforehand for this assembly was the subject of previous constitutional amendments.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if I understand your evidence correctly, you worked on a draft of another constitution. And was that submitted to this assembly that was held in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The political circumstances were such that probably somebody came to the conclusion that this form of constitution that we had advocated and proposed at that point in time in Borovo Selo, it would not have yielded any positive results. On the contrary, it would have brought about divisions. The basic concept, the basic difference in respect of this constitution in Borovo Selo was, according to our draft and that is the way it was supposed to be carried out, the president is elected by the assembly. There was this conglomerate of different relations in Borovo Selo. Some of this had been adopted and other things were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in your 2014 statement and this is paragraph 167, you state: "The constitutional powers of the RSK president under the constitution were very broad, especially in relation to the RSK's armed forces." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that constitution that was adopted, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. If we could have L55 on the screen. And I'm interested in the amendment 8, which to the left side. And for the English, we might need to go to page 2. Now you were shown this amendment number 8 to the RSK constitution during --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it please be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. This is what you were shown during direct examination last week, Mr. Susa. And it was promulgated on 18th May 1992. And we can see that it gave the RSK president -- president the power to appoint the RSK TO commander, as well as the power to appoint judges and prosecutors of the military courts. Now prior to this amendment, the RSK constitution did not expressly give the RSK president these powers, did it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Far wider powers were given to him as far as the TO commander was concerned. He could appoint and remove. This is a strange amendment, again some kind of political comprise. Now the president is only given the opportunity to appoint the TO commander. This is a very interesting situation. The already-existing TO commander cannot be replaced by the president. He could have been removed from that position only if he resigned himself or if, God forbid, he been killed. However, in a regular procedure, the president cannot have him removed from office.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, please speak slower so that the interpreters can understand you. I've looked at the constitution and I did not find any provision regarding the appointment of the TO commander or the appointment of military court judges or military prosecutors. Now we can look at Article 102 of the constitution, which this amendment amends, but I put to you that it does not deal with those particular issues. These are new powers given to the president.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are definitely not new powers. Why would the question of appointing the TO commander be raised in general when it is generally known? It can be seen from the constitution and the Law on Defence that the president appoints and dismisses. This president can no longer dismiss. He can only appoint. This is illogical.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we'll have to leave that there. The Judges do have the constitutes and they can see for themselves whether these powers were explicitly provided for in the constitution. Other than this amendment 8, the RSK president's constitutional powers in relation to the RSK armed forces remained unchanged until the 22nd of April 1993 when the constitutional amendments establishing the Supreme Defence Council were established; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council was a new limitation in terms of the breadth of the powers that the president had. When the Supreme Defence Council came into existence he became only a member of that council.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, because you're not answering my question. Between amendment number 8 and the amendment establishing the Supreme Defence Council there were no other constitutional changes that affected the RSK president's powers over the armed forces; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say right now, really. There were so many different amendments and different situations. I cannot recall. It would not be natural for me to be able to recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: While presiding over the Supreme Defence Council, Mr. Hadzic continued to assert himself as supreme commander of the RSK armed force, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're not going to be happy with my answer. But even until then, he was no supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's look at 65 ter 1800. This is tab 91. Now, unfortunately, I do not have a Serbian version of this article which is a 28 September 1993 Vecernje Novosti article, if I pronounced that correctly. In the beginning, Mr. Hadzic states to the press: "As supreme commander, I will carry out radical staffing changes in the army, leadership and the government. The reason for this is the recent developments on the Lika front." So I put to you again, Mr. Hadzic put himself out publicly as the commander of the armed forces, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no denying it that according to the position he held he was the supreme commander. I'm just saying how this functioned in reality. I'm not saying for a minute that he was not the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And at the end of this article, it reports that Mr. Hadzic: "Assessed the situation on the Lika front as stable, particularly after three strong units of the Krajina army had been deployed there. He then states that the demarcation line is the same as it was before." As president, Mr. Hadzic kept the public informed about the operations of the RSK armed forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no denying that he was duty-bound to do that in respect of everything except for what was a military secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 1800 will be Exhibit P3312.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic, as RSK president, attended RSK government sessions from time to time, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe a few times. I'm not ruling that out, but I am not linking it to anything significant that happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at 65 ter 1054. This is tab 49. And these are minutes from the RSK government session held on 27 to 28 April 1992. And we can see that both you and Goran Hadzic attended this session; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic was invited and was present, yes. It can be seen here that he was invited to attend the government session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we turn to page 3 of both the English and the Serbian version, the original version, we see that one of the decisions reached at the session was the creation of an RSK council for the protection of constitutional order. And we also see that Mr. Hadzic was appointed president of this council, which consisted of other high-ranking RSK officials; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 1054 will be Exhibit P3313.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have 1D2575 on the screen. This is tab 266.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And these are minutes of an RSK government session held on 14 July 1992. And, again, both you and Goran Hadzic are present at this session; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 7 of both versions. I'd like to draw your attention to item number 9. We see that after you provided reasons for consenting to the appointment of Djordje Calosevic as chairman of the Dalj Executive Council that consent was given to his appointment by the government; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D2575 will be Exhibit P3314.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The RSK president had the power to propose the appointment and the removal of the RSK prime minister, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. He could have made proposals, but it was the assembly that could remove the prime minister. I think that that was wrong and that this narrowed down the powers of the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us see 1D2619. And this is tab 269. This is a 17 March 1993 decision to appoint prime minister-elect to form a government. This is an example of Mr. Hadzic exercising his constitutional powers; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of proposing the prime minister-designate, yes. But he is not the one who appoints him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in March 1993, Mr. Hadzic also dismissed three ministers, including the minister of defence, Stojan Spanovic, as well as Mr. Bjegovic's predecessor as prime minister, Zdravko Zecevic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were dismissed by the government as its members, and Mr. Hadzic did not have these powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let look at paragraph 189 of your 2014 statement. And I'll read it for the record. You state: "Because of the failings of the defence and the heavy casualties sustained in this aggression," I think you're referring to the Maslenica incident, "the RSK president dismissed three ministers, including, minister of defence, Stojan Spanovic." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it's put a bit clumsily. However, when you see his powers this simply does not correspond to that. I was dismissed by the assembly at the assembly meeting, and that's the way it had to be. Maybe I misspoke, so please allow me to correct myself. There is really nothing there that is not written in documents so there's no need for me to invent anything here. Everything is written down in the documents. I may make a mistake though.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic was not pleased with what happened in Maslenica. The public was not pleased. And, as president, he took action by dismissing three ministers, as well as the prime minister, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, I'll move on. May this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 1D2619 will be Exhibit P3315.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have L38 on the screen. This is tab 21. Tab 21, this is L38.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Last week you testified about attending a government session in Erdut on 19 November. These are the minutes from that session; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are minutes from the session held on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, if I could draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. It was held on the 19th and the minutes were compiled on the 20th. I don't know why how come but all right I allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this meeting on 19 November in Erdut, it began in the morning and finished around 2.00 or 3.00 p.m.; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I don't know when it started. I don't know when it ended. Really.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, if you could look at paragraph 18 in your 1998 statement, does that first sentence refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time definitely. I must have remembered that better. I wouldn't correct it now. Probably when I stated that then, that is what was correct. I mean, it is correct now as well, but I no longer seem to remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now at this meeting, Goran Hadzic informed you and the other members of the government that he had talks with his associates who had returned from the terrain and that he was told that in the course of the following day, operations would be completed for the liberation of Vukovar; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did he mention who his associates were?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And at this 19 November 1991 session, it was decided to have a working and festive meeting, again the next day in Vukovar, which, in fact, happened at Velepromet; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this working and ceremonious meeting, I like that, so, yes, we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand your answer. Are you verifying what I asked you in the question?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We agreed that it would be a working and ceremonious meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition, and I believe this is what you describe in paragraph 16 of your 1998 statement: "The 19 November session was predominantly dedicated to the Vukovar events. One could feel certain euphoria since we had received information that the fights were nearly over with enemy forces being beaten. We were receiving this information at great speed. The news was delivered by the people who participated in the fighting or those originally coming from Vukovar, therefore, particularly interested in the situation. There were about 200 to 300 people who got together that day to discuss the situation." That was the situation, wasn't it, Mr. Susa?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And given the large number of persons present, the government was unable to follow a strict agenda on the 19th of November; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These 200 people could not even fit into the room where the government session was being held. When I refer to them, I mean the hallways and the rooms around the conference room where the government was meeting. I am not sure that they bothered us in our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But a strict agenda could not be followed that day, could it? And I'm looking at paragraph 18 of your statement at the very end of it.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's quite normal that the focus on work was weakened, but we did do some work.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at page 3 of the English of these minutes and page 4 of the original version. I would like to draw your attention ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the original version of the document only has two pages. Can counsel clarify, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely correct. I apologise for that. It's item 2 I'm interested in, which begins at the bottom of the page of these minutes and continues onto the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, and what I want to draw your attention to is that the minutes reflect that "Radovan Stojicic briefed those present on the military situation." And then after that, you and a number of other persons took part in that discussion. It was the case, Mr. Susa, wasn't it, that Badza provided the government with more information than mere casualty numbers. He provided information regarding the security situation.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This time, at the very end of the operations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, I apologise, I believe that the item is on page, yeah, 3 of the -- of the English, but we can look at that later. Now prior to the 20 November 1991 meeting at Velepromet, you knew that the SBWS government lacked a KP Dom prison in the Vukovar area which could house large numbers of prisoners from Vukovar; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It definitely didn't have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: There were only some makeshift collection centres, such as in Dalj and Borovo Selo; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about those collection centres. I never spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to the 20 November meeting, you and the other government members had been discussing at meetings and elsewhere stories about serious crimes allegedly committed against Serbs in Vukovar; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were not rumours. We had exact information from professionals who had a lot of experience in that work, had collected over the previous year. I'm talking about investigators, policemen, who spoke to families of the victims, survivors, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, given these stories -- and I use the word "stories" because that's the word you use in paragraph 29 of your 1998 statement. Given these stories that circulated, you were aware of the possibility that among the Serb population in Vukovar there may be a desire to seek revenge against captured Croat prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not suppose that on the basis of anything we knew. That's not a normal thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, during your Dokmanovic testimony, this is 1D2319, page 28 in e-court, which, again, Mr. Susa, you don't have in front of you, you testified that: "There were lots of internal settlings of accounts after the fall of Vukovar." Now you attributed this to Croatian formations but Serbs also had the desire to settle accounts in Vukovar against Croats, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know that. Those are only assumptions. And we didn't have even that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In your 1998 statement, this is paragraph 22, I state that you left Belgrade on the morning of 20 November, between 7.00 and 7.30 a.m. you accept that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, as I understand it, you travelled to Sid, and then from Sid you crossed over into the SBWS and went to Vukovar. Could you tell us how long did it take you to travel from Sid to Vukovar that morning?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, with all the circumstances around it, spending time there, picking up Bogdanovic, stopping in Sid, we needed three to three and a half hours to get to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I believe -- you said Belgrade. To Vukovar, I take it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean Vukovar. From Belgrade to Vukovar, three or three and a half hours with all the inevitable stops that were not short.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But I want to focus on the leg of your journey from Sid to Vukovar that morning. Could you give us an estimate of how long that took?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stopped by in Cakovac to see the brother of Bogdan Vojnovic. It's not important to the story, so I didn't mention it earlier. But passing through all the barricades and all that we needed to get through, I believe we travelled a little more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified last week that you needed a permit to enter the SBWS from Sid. Once you were inside the SBWS, you used your official SBWS government identification card to get through the army check-points; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was precisely that permit that I got previously in Sid. Everywhere where there was a military presence, where the military controlled traffic, I had to produce this permit I got from Sid. Only on the leg from Erdut to Dalj and in the area where we were known to people was I able to use my ID as a minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, if we look at paragraph 22 of your 1998 statement, you were talking about your journey to Vukovar that day. And you state: "I had my official ID card with me, which I would present but it meant nothing for a certain number of people." Then you go on to say: "Usually on our way to Vukovar my card always worked but this time, with much more efforts than usual." Now, in your statement, you only mention using your official ID and you make no mention of receiving a permit from Sid, and this is not something that you corrected in your 2014 statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this time I'm not even -- I'm even emphasizing here that my official ID was not enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's not correct. You say: "But this time, with much more efforts than usual."

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you get that additional permit in Sid. That was certainly so. I need not change anything here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you will agree that nowhere in this paragraph do you mention getting a permit from Sid.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the paragraph you are showing me, I don't see any mention of any permits, and I don't see that sentence you are citing. I say that at every check-point, my driver had to have a discussions, that I tried to calm him down, I produced my ID, but to a number of people, it meant nothing. When we went to Vukovar, my ID was usually enough, but this time, things were much harder. As far as I recall, that time we got a permit, a laissez-passer, in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That last part about the laissez-passer in Sid, that's not in that paragraph. Let's be clear about that.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not in this paragraph. But if you will, treat it as if we got a permit in Sid, although it won't be correct. Use that part of my statement whichever way is convenient to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified that you arrived at Vukovar around 10.30 a.m. and you arrived at the Velepromet 60 to 70 minutes later. This was last week during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean we arrived at Vukovar at 10.30 and we took another 60 minutes to travel to Vukovar? I didn't say that. That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question because maybe something was lost in it. You testified last week that you arrived Vukovar around 10.30; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then you testified about how you engaged in some other activities and that you arrived at the Velepromet facility 60 to 70 minutes after arriving in Vukovar; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was close to noon when we got back to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, based upon your testimony last week, you arrived at Velepromet somewhere around 11.30 to 11.40 a.m. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you testified that when you arrived at Velepromet you saw Goran Hadzic, Arkan, and Vitomir Devetak, as well as Bogdan Vojnovic in the yard of Velepromet. This is from your testimony last week. Now, in your statement from 1998, you also mention seeing Mladen Hadzic, Slavko Dokmanovic, Rade Leskovac and Bogdan Vorkapic in the yard as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's obviously a mistake. Bogdan Vojnovic was the man who was with me all the time. We never separated. I didn't see him in the yard because he was with me. This is probably about Bogdan Vorkapic, and it's just a mistake. Maybe it doesn't matter but Bogdan Vojnovic was with me all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. I accept that. But what I wanted to verify is that in additional to seeing Goran Hadzic and Arkan in the yard you also saw Mladen Hadzic, Slavko Dokmanovic, Rade Leskovac and, as you just mentioned, Bogdan Vorkapic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Them, and many other people who were standing in the yard. Behind the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then you testified that you waited an hour before you entered the Velepromet offices; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably even longer. People were standing in clusters and talking. It's very difficult for me to determine how much time we actually spent that way. It could be an hour, it could be more.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, turning to the meeting itself, a majority of the members of the SBWS government attended the Velepromet meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them, yes. But a number was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question wasn't most -- well, I think that answered it. So at least a majority was present; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the last words of the witness were not transcribed or interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Susa.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What specifically do you mean? What am I supposed to repeat? That the majority was there? Yes, the majority, I believe, was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And Arkan also attended the meeting and he sat next to Goran Hadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to my left. I believe between them and our table, there was another table.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you assumed that Arkan came to Vukovar that day escorting Goran Hadzic since the section between Erdut and Vukovar was still highly unsafe; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a logical assumption and my inference. Nobody told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It was also your personal opinion that on that day, Arkan had come to strengthen the position of Goran Hadzic during his encounter with military leaders; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you testified last week that at the Velepromet meeting, there were several military officers present that you did not know. It is possible that some of those military officers who were present were TO commanders; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were different from officers because they didn't have such ranks. Our TO officers almost didn't have any ranks, and these other officers had one or two stars, or some insignia showing a different rank. That's why I inferred they did not belong to the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's look at your Dokmanovic testimony. This is 1D2319, page 53. And you were asked: "Were Territorial Defence commanders also present in this meeting on the 20th of November?" And then you stated: "It is possible that some of the commanders were there."

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not questioning it even now. I distinguished them from the officers. In the room where we held the meeting, there was a number of people who were coming in and out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In your 1998 statement, you stated that Veselin Sljivancanin joined the meeting and even spoke at it, but your testimony in this case was that he only peeked through the door; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, sorry. I didn't testify that he spoke. Veselin Sljivancanin, and I believe said that in 1998 as well, just peeked through the door. He was not very well known from the media and then he left. Veselin Sljivancanin, definitely didn't attend this meeting, nor did he say a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I wasn't referring to your previous testimony. I was referring to your 1998 statement. In that statement you stated that Sljivancanin was -- attended the meeting and you've changed that testimony, that he only peeked in; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I maintained that he did not attend the meeting. And I don't know how such a mistake occurred in the interpretation of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified last week that a lieutenant-colonel at the meeting introduced himself as Vojnovic. And if you look at your 1998 statement, paragraph 27, you described the military officer present at the meeting as "holding the rank of a colonel." Why now have you demoted him to lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I don't know if he was a lieutenant-colonel or a colonel, and it's completely irrelevant. I know that he introduced himself as Vojnovic. It's possible that he was a lieutenant-colonel. I totally didn't care about this. I didn't pay attention. It was totally unimportant to me. I saw several stars on his shoulder strap. I don't know if I counted them correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You also state in your 1998 statement - and this is paragraph 31 - that you were not sure that the name of the colonel was Vojnovic. Why are you now so certain that his name was Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still not sure whether his name is Vojnovic or Vojinovic. When a person introduces himself, he says his name only once, and you may not hear properly. I'm still not sure whether he's Vojnovic or Vojinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have D220 on the screen. This photograph was shown to you during direct examination. In your 2014 statement, in paragraph 115, you state that this image appears at time code 14:05 hours on a video dated 20 November 1991. If you turn to paragraph 44 of your 1998 statement, which is at the very end, you will see that in this statement, you were shown this video, which was taken outside of Velepromet, and you identified a number of people in the video from time code 13:49 to 15:12 hours. However, you will see in your statement that you did not identify Bogdan Vujic, did you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the previous and in this statement, I definitely identified Colonel Vujovic, whom I know personally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure whether it's Vujic or Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I believe you said Colonel Vujic; correct? Vujic.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it's just to clarify the record, Mr. Susa. But I want you to look at paragraph 44 of your 1998 statement, not your 2014 statement, Mr. Susa. And in this statement, as I will repeat, you were shown this video from time code 13:49 all the way to 15:12 and yet you never identified Colonel Vujic in that footage, did you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't see it well. Maybe it's not in that footage. I don't know what you're talking about. I'm telling you again I was then shown a picture of Bogdan Vujic and I identified him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who showed you this particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I testified back in the Slavko Dokmanovic case, this photograph was shown to me, and you showed it again to me now. It was shown to me in these proceedings as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We have your transcript from your Dokmanovic testimony and at least during your testimony you were not shown this photograph. Can you tell us who is the one who showed you this photograph that's in front of us?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this photograph was shown to me last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: By Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mr. Zivanovic showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted. We'll take the first break, 30 minutes. We will be back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, you have something like 40 minutes left, you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, if I understand correctly, 45 minutes, and I think I should be able to do it within that time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, last week you testified that Mladen Hadzic interrupted the colonel's report on the security situation in Vukovar at the Velepromet meeting. In fact, it was Goran Hadzic who interrupted the JNA officer's presentation in the course -- or his report on the course of finalizing the military operation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Mladen Hadzic did not interrupt this man. He let him speak. And then he attacked him. That was not Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, if we look at paragraph 28 of your 1998 statement, you state: "We took our seats and this military officer started the meeting in describing the course of finalizing military operations when Hadzic interrupted him. In my opinion, the meeting was clearly presided over by this colonel, and I think that at one point, Hadzic even declined to sit besides the colonel. Anyway, Hadzic said his speech was irrelevant at the moment ..." It goes from there. That's Goran Hadzic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Mladen Hadzic, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that it was Mladen Hadzic who declined to sit besides the colonel?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was next to him anyway, and, at that moment, I realised that he would refuse to sit next to him. He distanced -- distanced himself about 2 metres away before he started speaking. Hadzic was already sitting in his own seat and he was not next to the colonel, or lieutenant-colonel. Now I mean Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, take a look at paragraph 29 of your statement. You know, in this paragraph, you state at the very beginning: "I can remember that Dr. Mladen Hadzic delivered a rather emotional speech, talking about the information from the places where abductions and identifications of dead bodies were conducted." So in this paragraph, when you're referring to Dr. Hadzic, or Dr. Mladen Hadzic, you referred to him by his full name, and I put to you in your statement when you referred to Goran Hadzic, you simply referred to him as Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That could not be inferred on the basis of these parts that are marked here as 25, where I specifically refer to Goran Hadzic. It's quite possible that someone did not record the name of Mladen Hadzic, who is the person I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, the paragraph we just looked at suggests, and I believe your testimony also suggested, that at this meeting, emotions were running high; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, in fact, you reminded everyone present at the meeting about the stories of crimes that took place, including many cases of violent death, rapes and burning of houses; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I added onto what the colonel said at the moment when he said that all prisoners would be exchanged. That is what I was speaking of at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, look at paragraph 29, and after you describe what Dr. Mladen Hadzic stated, you state: "I myself joined the discussion by reminding the others on the stories about the crimes that took place and the facts we were familiar with concerning many cases of violent deaths, et cetera." You were referring to crimes against Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant all crimes. So if we are to be honest, I particularly meant crimes against Serbs that had been totally uninvestigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And at the time, just from your last answer, you and the SBWS government were aware that crimes had been committed against the non-Serb population in Vukovar; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could assume that. We didn't know anything for sure. Not in terms of our crimes or these crimes. All of that had to be investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, at a certain point during this meeting, the military officer, presumably the colonel, also said something that added to the already tense atmosphere, by pointing out that the army would prevent any form of possible revenge and vengefulness; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one spoke of revenge and vengefulness. And, in that sense, the colonel, or lieutenant-colonel, didn't have to intervene. He just stated that prisoners were under the most direct control of the military than they would be transferred to different locations. All of that was all right and in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's look at paragraph 28 of your 1998 statement. I draw your attention to the last sentence of paragraph 28 where you state: "At a certain point, the military officer also said something that added to the already tense atmosphere, by pointing out that the army would prevent any form of possible revenge and vengefulness." That's what you stated in your 1998 statement. And that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not going to deny that. All of that is fine. But I don't know what caused what he did and said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the topic of the non-Serb prisoners of war who were captured during the Vukovar operation, you, Goran Hadzic, Mladen Hadzic, and Slavko Dokmanovic, as well as a few additional government members, took part in that discussion; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in that. I think that Mladen Hadzic did not. That Slavko Dokmanovic did not. And Goran Hadzic said a few sentences about all of that just before he left the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, that is different from what you said in your 2014 statement, but I'll move on. Mr. Hadzic, Goran Hadzic, at this meeting, insisted that there were serious criminals among the prisoners of war who had to be found and brought before the courts; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he actually said that among the prisoners of war, most people were innocent. In that way, he was referring to what Colonel or Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic was saying. And he had interpreted that to us in a way that was not really important to us. No one said that most prisoners of war had or had not committed crimes. Goran Hadzic said that a small group of people had committed crimes and he said that we are not equating all Croats to war criminals. And that's when he left the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll draw your attention to paragraph 30 of your 1998 statement where you state: "At the initial stage and even later it was the military authorities who were exclusively in charge of the issue of prisoners of war. That was normal. And no one had any comments about that except Hadzic," which I assume you mean Goran Hadzic, "who pointed out that there were for sure many innocent people but there was also serious criminals who had to be discovered and put on trial." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what he was saying just before he left the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now you testified last week that Goran Hadzic stated at this meeting: "We do not identify the Croatian people with criminals and we are perfectly aware that we will have to peacefully coexist in the future." Mr. Susa, I put to you that you made no mention of this statement by Mr. Hadzic in your 1998 statement, your 2014 statement, or during your Dokmanovic testimony. The first time you have provided evidence regarding this statement about peaceful co-existence was before this Trial Chamber in this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that this is the first time I've said this, but that is true, and Goran spoke and wrote about this a few days beforehand. I think that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified last week that you protested that no checks were being performed on the prisoners of war to determine whether they had committed war crimes. In fact, you stated at this meeting that you wanted those checks and those investigations to be performed by the local police and judiciary so that the prisoners could be brought to justice in the SBWS; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've oversimplified this and you have reduced my statement completely. I said that investigations had to be carried out so that the perpetrators of crimes could be identified. I did not protest at all. There was no reason for any kind of protest at that point in time, except for the statement of Colonel Vojnovic that everyone would be exchanged on an all-for-all basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you wanted those investigations, those checks, to be conducted inside the SBWS before the prisoners left your jurisdiction; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. We clearly stated that at these places where this would be carried out, if it is carried out, we want our people to be present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next thing I want to deal with the witness should not see it. It should not be broadcasted to the public as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The document shall not be shown to the witness and not be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't think you mentioned the document number, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll do so now. It's P3204. This is tab 130. And if we could -- if we could turn to page 27, I'm interested in paragraph 143. And I mean in the English version. I'm not sure what page it is on the Serbian version. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. According to this statement, which you won't be able to see, Mr. Susa, it was mentioned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness. His microphone seems to be off.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, according to this statement: "It was mentioned at the meeting at Velepromet that the military-aged male prisoners, some in uniforms and some not, were taken to Sremska Mitrovica and some other towns, Major Sljivancanin said that these men would take them until it was clear to they were and what they did. That is what Susa was referring to when he said we had the police and we had judiciary, and we could do it on our own. Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was opposed to these men being sent to Sremska Mitrovica." Mr. Susa it is correct, isn't it, that you insisted at the meeting that the SBWS police and judiciary should carry out proceedings against the prisoners on their own?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not. There was no reason for that, and there weren't any conditions for that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In your statement, you -- this is your 1998 statement, you state that at the meeting also Arkan said a few things which were not worth remembering. I think this is in paragraph 30. In fact, what Arkan said was that the prisoners must remain in the SBWS, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Arkan said is really not worth remembering. I'd forgotten that. He didn't speak about that, though. I would have remembered that because that is a rather serious matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen D187. This should also not be broadcast to the witness. D187. This is tab 263. And if we could turn to page 9. I'm interested in paragraph 48. Now, in this statement, it states: "The main issue that was being discussed was whether some people who had been arrested should be taken to Serbia. Some people claimed that there was a judiciary in the region and their guilt should be established there. I think it was Vojo Susa that was saying this." That's correct, isn't it, you were saying that at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just in part, as I have already explained. Once investigations are carried out and once evidence is compiled, the trial could be held in Vukovar as well. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen 65 ter 6685 and still do not broadcast this to the witness at the moment. This is tab 173. And if we could turn to page 4 in both versions. And if we could enlarge the -- the original version somewhat, the best we can. Yeah, that's fine. And now if we could broadcast this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, I put to you that these are notes from the 20 November meeting of the government at Velepromet, and you'll see that the second, I guess paragraph, indicates that someone by the name of Vojo stated: "They are not the prisoners of war." It is you who made that statement; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are showing me a slip of paper from a little notebook that is carried around by military intelligence people. This is not any kind of minutes or record. This is not the area where we were at the time. This has no official character. Anybody could have written this at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But you didn't answer my question. My question is: The statement made "they are not the prisoners of war," you made that statement at the Velepromet meeting, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were prisoners of war. I knew that, and I could not have stated anything like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was there anyone with the nickname Vojo at that meeting that you recall?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The notes then indicate that the minister of the interior stated: "We waged the war together. We should put them on trial together. "This people and the government should have been consulted on how to put them on trial and where. "Only over the citizens' dead bodies is it going to be possible to leave Vukovar for Sremska Mitrovica with the Ustashas." Mr. Susa, that is what Borislav Bogunovic said regarding the matter of the prisoners, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borislav Bogunovic did not speak about that. I'm sure that he did not speak about that at all. I am sure that he did not speak at all. Therefore, he couldn't have said this either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object. I would object. First of all, we don't know who is author of this document. We -- we -- we saw the name of -- on the first page of this witness statement this -- this witness was known to the Prosecution for at least ten years. He was not put on their list. We had no opportunity to cross-examine him, if he is author of -- of this document. And, because of that, I object to tendering of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The first part of this document is a statement authenticating this document which was recently obtained by the Prosecution. The sole purpose of that statement is to authenticate the nature of this document. And this document itself has been on the Prosecution's 65 ter list. It just required authentication that which was recently obtained, and our position is that the document goes to the weight of not only this witness as to what happened at the Velepromet meeting but other witnesses as well, and therefore, the document itself can be admitted, and the statement is simply there to assist the Trial Chamber in a -- evaluating its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is my position that we have full right to cross-examine this witness who allegedly made this document and to see when he made -- made this document and whether he made this document. This witness, I repeat, was known to the Prosecution for ten years, and he was not put on their list. He was not called as a witness in their case. And I object. In addition, since the witness could not confirm anything about this document, I object it -- for this reasons, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I just point out that the document doesn't go directly to the acts and conduct of the accused. It does not mention Mr. Hadzic himself and therefore we believe it can be tendered for the purpose that the Prosecution is presenting it for. With regard to the issue of whether the provider of this document should come for cross-examination or direct examination, that's an issue that can always be raised down the road. As Your Honours has mentioned with regard to other documents that the Defence have added to their list that may require re-call of a witness or calling of an additional witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I -- my position is we would be deprived, really deprived, to -- of our rights, of the rights of the accused to cross-examine the witness who allegedly made this document, and who -- who -- allegedly stated and gave just one piece of paper from his alleged book, notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, can we have the first page on the screen. Not for the public and not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll just have to turn off the monitors and then ... certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And perhaps the witness should take his head phone off for a moment, please. We are not quite sure we understand, Mr. Olmsted. This seems to be a witness statement by the author of the notebook; is that right?
